# High-pressure steam engine (`high_pressure_steam`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: needs safety_valve_boiler; helped by boring_machine, atmospheric_engine, crank_connecting_rod, rolling_mill, puddling_wrought_iron, lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: Let the steam itself push the piston, at several atmospheres above ambient pressure. In a simple non-condensing engine the exhaust goes to the open air; other high-pressure engines use condensers. Atmospheric exhaust saves the weight of a condenser, its air pump and its cooling-water supply. A greater pressure difference gives more piston force for the same bore, making compact mobile engines practical. Everything now depends on the boiler: a cylindrical shell of small diameter, in riveted wrought-iron plate, with the fire in a flue through the water, two safety valves and a fusible plug. Letting the steam expand after an early cut-off, or passing it through a second larger cylinder (compounding), takes more work from each charge before exhaust. A condenser improves economy in a different way by reducing exhaust back-pressure. Turning the exhaust up the chimney draws the fire.
- Pitfalls:
  - Raising the pressure on a boiler built for a low-pressure engine
  - Cast-iron boilers and fastened-down safety valves: the Greenwich explosion of 1803 killed four men
  - Believing Watt's separate-condenser patent covered every use of high-pressure steam; a non-condensing engine could operate without his patented condenser
  - Joints, glands and piston packing made as for low pressure; they blow out
- History: europe: 1720s – Leupold publishes a design for a high-pressure, non-condensing engine; 1769 Cugnot's steam gun carriage in Paris; 1799–1802 Richard Trevithick's 'puffer' engines in Cornwall, road carriage (Camborne, 1801) and patent; 1804 his locomotive at Penydarren; 1804 Woolf's compound engine; 1812 Cornish engine and boiler; americas: 1801–1804 – Oliver Evans in Philadelphia builds high-pressure engines independently and publishes the principles in 1805
- Read:
  - Oliver Evans, The Abortion of the Young Steam Engineer's Guide (1805)
  - Anthony Burton, Richard Trevithick: Giant of Steam (2000)
  - Richard L. Hills, Power from Steam: A History of the Stationary Steam Engine (1989)
